articles.title: Show Your Work: Platforms Must Make Safety Decisions That Brands Can Verify
articles.fullContent:
“Human or machine?” is the wrong question. The right one is: Can you see the work?

Detailed written rules reduced measured ambiguity in content decisions from 18% to 7%.

X is building visibility into safety decisions and allowing authors to appeal them.

Beta · Generated by AI, reviewed by ADWEEK newsroom This column is adapted from the keynote address that X Head of Safety Michael O’Herlihy gave at the recent Brand and AI Safety Summit.

When I was at school in Ireland, math exams had a rule I thought was deeply unfair. You were allowed to just write down the answer—but if the answer was wrong, you got nothing. Zero.

However, if you showed your work, and your method was right but you’d slipped on one line, you still got partial credit.

It took me years to see the point. Showing your work doesn’t just give people an answer. It helps them understand how you got there. An answer on its own asks for trust; showing the work lets you check it.

I’ve spent two decades in the business of judgment calls: what stays up, what comes down, what is eligible for reach. Every one of those judgments is an answer. And for most of that time, our industry has handed people the answer and kept the work hidden. For too long, this has been a black box.

People ask me who makes better calls, humans or machines. Both make mistakes. If you give the same post to a hundred trained reviewers, you won’t get a hundred identical answers. So “human or machine?” is the wrong question. The right one is: Can you see the work?

Today, mostly, you can’t see inside. The systems that decide what you see, and what sits next to an ad, run out of sight. The deal was “trust us.” It held while volumes were manageable, and it stopped working as they grew.

Here’s the good news. AI doesn’t just make decisions faster. It gives us new ways to make those decisions explainable and testable. We now have the opportunity to turn the black box into a glass box: decisions you can trace back to the rules, and people outside who can check them, challenge them and help us improve them.

But a glass box alone doesn’t make a system safe. You could fill one with bad decisions. It would just let people see them. So transparency on its own isn’t the standard—defensibility is. Can this decision be justified under the rules? Transparency provides the evidence: Can someone see how we got there? Verification is the test: Can someone outside check whether the system consistently follows the rules?

Before returning to X, I worked at Reddit, where my colleague Rosa Català and I published a paper earlier this year called Escaping the Agreement Trap: Defensibility Signals for Evaluating Rule-Governed AI.

The usual test for a content-decision system is whether it agreed with a human. Same answer, pass. Different answer, fail. We looked at more than 193,000 real content decisions from Reddit and asked whether each one could be traced back to the written rules.

When the model and the human disagreed, the usual assumption is that the model got it wrong. But roughly four out of five of those model decisions could still be defended under the written rules. Disagreement doesn’t necessarily mean the model was wrong. Often, both opposing decisions were defensible. Grading by agreement is the wrong exam entirely: checking the answer, never the working.

How can two opposite decisions both be defensible? Ambiguity. Two reasonable people can look at the same case, reach opposite conclusions, and both be within the rules. Some ambiguity isn’t a bug, it’s what happens when real people apply rules to real life. But a lot of it can be managed, and it starts with more detailed rules. When we gave the model detailed written rules instead of just bullets, measured ambiguity dropped from 18% to 7%.

So how do we actually build the glass box? One window at a time.

Window one: See how it’s ranked. We open-sourced the For You algorithm, the system behind the feed: ranking, filtering and visibility-limiting labels. It’s on GitHub, and we keep it updated to match what’s running on X. Anyone can read it; you get the code, not a blog post about the code.

Window two: Add context. That’s Community Notes, where contributors can add context to any post. A note is only shown publicly if enough contributors from different points of view rate it helpful. The algorithm is open, and so is the data. Context comes from the community, not from us.

Window three: See what applies to your account. My colleague Keith Coleman’s team built Under the Hood. It shows account holders the visibility decisions that apply to them, and any restrictions applied due to a government request or court order. You don’t have to guess. You can look.

Window four: Understand the decision. This is what we’re building in Safety. Not just making decisions visible, but giving people clear ways to understand them, challenge them and help us get them right. When we label a post, the author will be able to tap the label and see what it was based on, in plain language, not code or model internals. They’ll see what it means for reach: who it won’t be recommended to, and who will see it behind a warning. And they’ll be able to appeal, telling us what we should have seen, so we can take another look and fix it if we got it wrong.

Sometimes people will still disagree, and that’s fine. Agreement was never the goal. What we want to hear is, “I still disagree, but I see why you got there.” A mistake you can see is a mistake you can fix. But there is a limit.

The glass box shows the rules and the decisions, not the answer key. We don’t publish the signals and thresholds we use to catch spam, scams and coordinated abuse. Open enough to verify. Closed enough that it can’t be gamed.

The past few years have tested advertiser confidence across the industry, and no platform, including X, is exempt from that scrutiny. That skepticism is legitimate, and the right response isn’t to ask for trust back. It’s to make trust earnable. Brands need to understand the decisions that shape where their ads appear, because what’s allowed on a platform and what you want next to your ad are two different standards.

The X platform philosophy of “ Freedom of Speech, Not Reach ” is built on that distinction. Lawful speech can stay up without being amplified. But limited reach should never mean hidden decisions.

Our rules decide what’s allowed; ranking decides what we recommend. Suitability decides what sits next to a brand, and that’s the brand’s call, not ours. Every brand draws that line differently; advertisers shouldn’t have to accept someone else’s definition of what’s suitable for them.

Control means setting your own standard. Transparency means seeing where your ads appear. Independent measurement means verifying whether it’s working. Published rules tell you what should happen. Transparency shows you what happened.

But neither, on its own, proves that a system is working consistently at scale. Verification does. Platforms shouldn’t be the only ones grading their own work, which is why at X we partner with DoubleVerify and Integral Ad Science.

To the platforms: Show your work. Write rules clear enough that decisions can be traced back to them, and let people outside your walls check the results.

To brands and agencies: Ask for it. Make “Can I check this?” a normal question, and ask every platform, including X: Can I set my own suitability standard? Can I see where my ads actually ran? Who outside your company checks it? Safety shouldn’t be something platforms ask you to trust. It should be something you can verify.

articles.title: 5 Black Friday Truths About Gen Z Shoppers and the Mall
articles.fullContent:
Gen Z shoppers not only spend more time at the mall, but they spend more too.

Gen Z is choosing physical shopping after growing up on ecommerce.

Three in five Gen Z mall visitors come primarily to socialize rather than shop—yet there's still an opportunity for brands.

Beta · Generated by AI, reviewed by ADWEEK newsroom Welcome to Black Friday—the start of the most critical five days of the year for retail brands.

According to Circana, 43% of Americans will do most of their holiday shopping between today and Monday, and nearly a quarter of them will do most of it today, full stop.

This is also the day that brands are focused on Gen Z, because 94% of them plan to shop this week, according to Deloitte, and they’ll spend an average of $752—more than any other age cohort.

It’s a given that many consumers aged 14-29 will spend that money online. But a lot of shopping is also going to happen at the place Gen X made famous: the mall.

You’ll find plenty of zoomers in malls today, in fact, but they’re not all spending the way you think, and some aren’t there to shop at all. ADWEEK waded through a stack of recent market studies and tapped the shoulders of a few experts to plumb Gen Z’s current relationship with the mall and what it means for Black Friday 2026.

Gen X might have been the original mall rats in the 1980s, but today’s 18-29 age group has picked up the mantle.

According to Coresight research released in April, 48% of Gen Z consumers say they’ve hit the mall in the last two weeks. A recent Ipsos survey found that shoppers aged 18-34 were twice as likely as those 55 and up to shop at the mall. And according to a Stagwell study released this year, Gen Z not only spends more time at the mall on a per-visit basis, they also spend $296 per visit on average, the most of any age group.

Gen Z mall affinity seems strongest with women, too. A 2026 study of female zoomers’ shopping activity conducted by snack maker Sunnie and Westfield Rise found that 86% of them praised the mall for giving them “energy they can’t get digitally.”

2. The analog renaissance extends to shopping

The reasons why Gen Z likes the mall have as much to do with what the mall is as what it’s not—a small screen. Mall shopping represents a rebound effect in retail form, a response to hours of isolated scrolling.

Coresight’s work states it plainly. “Gen Z has grown up with frictionless digital commerce as a baseline expectation,” researchers wrote, “yet precisely because of this ubiquity, they increasingly seek the tangible, social and experiential dimensions of physical retail.”

It’s worth noting that experts are also starting to see the same dynamic unfolding with Gen Alpha (aged 13 and under), whose spending power and influence is already approaching $100 billion , per Charles Schwab.

“A trip to the mall with friends can be an important first taste of autonomy,” Helenor Gilmour, head of marketing research firm Beano Brain, told ADWEEK. “That shared experience is a powerful part of the appeal of shopping in stores. It is why we expect younger shoppers to embrace shopping events like Black Friday as a reason to visit malls together.”

Brieane Olson, CEO of PacSun, is well positioned to observe the evolving shopping habits of Gen Z. The brand sells its apparel online, in freestanding stores, and at mall locations. It’s easy to assume that a generation that grew up with ecommerce would stick to what they know; or they might defect because they’re tired of it. But the truth lay in between.

“We’re continuing to see just how important physical retail is to young consumers, and there’s a real opportunity for malls heading into Black Friday and the holiday season,” Olson told ADWEEK. “Young people aren’t choosing between digital and physical experiences. They want both, and they expect brands to create meaningful connections across each.”

4. Gen Z looks for online culture at the mall

With over 520 stores across 4.2 million square feet and sales north of $650 million a year, Bloomington, Minnesota’s Mall of America (MOA) is the biggest mall in the continental U.S. According to its 2026 Holiday Shopping Survey, 92% of Gen Z respondents expressed an intent to show up there today, with over half saying they planned to spend once they arrive.

Just as significantly, MOA has charted a symbiotic relationship between the online culture Gen Z consumes and their behavior when they visit.

“Social media may introduce them to a brand, trend or community, but there’s still an appeal to experiencing those interests firsthand,” said a MOA spokesperson. “We’re seeing that with our leasing strategy. Brands such as Edikted and Pop Mart , along with concepts like Bandai Namco and Kpop Nara, reflect how interests that develop online are translating into physical retail experiences.”

“Gen Z may discover what’s next online,” MOA chief business development and marketing officer Jill Renslow added, “but they still want to experience it together in the real world.”

From a brand perspective, it’s not enough that Gen Z merely visits the mall—retailers still need to woo them once they get there.

According to the International Council of Shopping Centers, 60% of Gen Z mall visitors say they go “ just to socialize or meet friends.” Sunnie and Westfield North’s work found that 72% of female zoomers would still visit the mall even if it meant they couldn’t buy anything.

But there’s still a marketing opportunity here. Coresight’s study determined that social-media content creation is a big reason for mall visits, calling them “aesthetically curated spaces [that] serve as backdrops for organic and shareable moments.”

The brands that benefit most, said the study, are those that boast “visually engaging environments with Instagrammable decor.”

Robert Klara is the senior editor of brands at Adweek, specializing in the evolution and impact of brands.

  1. Influencer marketing is a fast-growing market. The global influencer marketing platform market is projected to reach $97.55 billion by 2030, up from a projected $34.25 billion in 2025.

Influencer marketing is a social media strategy where brands partner with content creators to promote their products or services to their engaged audience. It’s a projected $12.17 billion market in the U.S. alone, and it sits inside almost every major brand’s media plan now.

Think of it as digital word-of-mouth marketing — instead of your neighbor raving about their new air fryer over the fence, it’s someone with 20,000 TikTok followers influencing your next purchasing decision.

Celebrity endorsements were the original form of creator partnership. But today, social content creators with niche audiences can be even more powerful marketing tools.

These influencers often have stronger relationships with their followers, making their recommendations more impactful.

Source: Grand View Research

In other words, there’s no one-size-fits-all approach to making influencer marketing work. With the right social media strategy and research, just about every brand’s message can benefit from a little influencer amplification.

articles.title: What is a sponsored post? Types and examples (2026)
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Sponsored posts include any social media content a brand pays to promote, either through platform ad tools (a boosted post) or through an influencer partnership.
  2. Each platform has its own tools and labels for sponsored content, from Instagram’s paid partnership label to TikTok’s Spark Ads and LinkedIn’s Campaign Manager.
  3. FTC disclosure rules require clear and conspicuous labelling on all paid content. Non-compliance can lead to enforcement action against both the brand and the creator.
  4. Measuring ROI takes UTM parameters, unique discount codes, and platform analytics. Likes and comments alone won’t tell you whether a campaign paid for itself.

What is a sponsored post?

A sponsored post is any social media post you’ve paid to promote. When you create a sponsored post, you’re spending money to help it reach a wider audience.

“Sponsored post” works as an umbrella term. It covers posts you pay a platform to distribute, posts you pay a creator to publish, and editorial-style branded content produced with a publisher or partner. What they share is money changing hands to get a message in front of people who wouldn’t have seen it organically.

Platforms label these posts so users can tell the difference. Facebook and LinkedIn mark paid placements as “Sponsored” or “Promoted,” Instagram uses a “Paid partnership with [brand]” tag above creator posts, and TikTok adds a disclosure to content flagged with its branded content toggle. In the US, those labels sit alongside Federal Trade Commission rules that require disclosure of any material connection between a brand and a creator.

You can find sponsored posts on every social media platform, including Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, and even LinkedIn.

There are three main types of sponsored posts, and they differ in who creates the content, where it appears, and how it gets labelled.

1. Promoted or boosted posts

This is the traditional style of paid advertisement. Brands pay to publish native ads on a social platform like Instagram or Facebook. Paid ads use data like location, age, or interests to target specific audiences. Your ad money goes directly to the social media platform.

Boosted posts are easy to spot because they have the word “sponsored” or “promoted” underneath the account username. Paid posts often feature a call-to-action button to drive results, such as “Shop Now” or “Download.”

articles.title: 40 Pinterest stats that matter to marketers in 2026
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Pinterest reached 631 million monthly active users in Q1 2026, its tenth straight quarter of double-digit growth.
  2. Women make up 70% of users, and Gen Z is the platform’s fastest-growing audience.
  3. Pinterest users run more than 80 billion searches a month and are nearly 90% more likely than users on other platforms to say they’re ready to shop.
  4. Only 22% of companies market on Pinterest, which means less competition and lower ad costs for brands that show up.

1. As of Q1 2026, Pinterest has 631 million monthly active users (MAUs)

631 million people use Pinterest every month, up 11% year over year. That marks the tenth straight quarter of double-digit user growth.

For marketers, that steady climb in monthly active users means a bigger, more reliable audience to reach, and a sign Pinterest isn’t going anywhere.

It scored 78 on the American Customer Satisfaction Index (a measure of how satisfied US consumers are with a service) in 2025, beating Instagram, TikTok, and Facebook.

That goodwill matters. When people actually enjoy being on a platform, they’re more receptive to the content and brands they run into there, which makes Pinterest a friendlier place to market than the platforms people love to complain about.

articles.title: How Does Substack Work? A Beginner’s Guide
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Substack lets you publish newsletters and other content, including videos and podcasts, that readers can follow on the platform or receive by email when they subscribe. 
  • Creators can build an audience through free subscriptions and choose which content to reserve for paying subscribers. 
  • Creators can publish on Substack for free. If they offer paid subscriptions, Substack takes 10 percent of subscription revenue, plus payment-processing fees. 
  • Growing an audience requires consistent publishing and active reader engagement. 
  • Paid subscriptions work best when creators offer content readers find valuable enough to pay for.

Substack isn’t just another content platform. It’s a powerful tool for building and monetizing a community.

Substack works by providing a user-friendly way to create and monetize your ideas with tools that attract engaged subscribers. There are more than 5 million paid subscribers on the platform, with tens of millions of people engaging with Substack content each week.

With Substack’s built-in community features, those users can discover your content, too.

The best part? You don’t need a huge audience or technical skills to get started. You just need something worth saying and the consistency to show up.

I’ll walk you through how to use Substack’s features to establish yourself as a voice in your space and create a path to monetization.

What Is Substack?

Substack is a publishing platform where creators and brands can produce, distribute, and monetize digital content. 

Although it started as a platform for written content, Substack users now produce content in several media formats. You can use it to distribute content like podcasts, newsletters, and videos to your audience.

Take Lenny Rachitsky, for example. This top-ranked business creator reaches 1.2 million subscribers through newsletters and podcasts published on Substack.

On the surface, Substack might seem like a standard email newsletter platform. However, it’s designed to encourage engagement.

Substack Notes lets users share short posts and interact with others, much like a social media feed. 

Substack Chat gives creators a space to have conversations with their subscribers. 

Going live allows conversations to happen in real time. 

These all encourage organic discussion threads.

Recommending other content on Substack also builds community and encourages engagement with fellow writers.

With Substack, creators have tons of ways to connect with followers. I’ll walk you through these features below.

How Does Substack Work?

Substack works as a subscription-based model. Followers can subscribe to content creators and receive email or in-app notifications when they publish something new.

Creators can set up one or more subscription tiers, including free and paid. Below, I’ll show you how paid tiers work.

Unlike standard email newsletters, with Substack, your content goes to inboxes, the creator’s feed in the Substack app, and the website. 

Think of it as a blog, email newsletter, and social network all rolled into one.

The Subscription and Distribution Model

When you hit publish on Substack, three things happen. Your newsletter:
 

  • Lands in your subscribers’ inboxes
  • Appears in the Substack app inbox
  • Goes live on your publication page

This distribution model makes it easier for your content to be found, shared, and liked. 

If readers or other creators like your content, they can choose to subscribe. Subscriptions are the lifeblood of Substack and the best way to share your content and grow your audience. 

Subscriptions can be free or paid (more on that later). Unless you already have a large following, start with free content to grow your subscriber list. Content that doesn’t charge subscribers doesn’t have a Substack platform fee, so it’s free for you, too.

How Substack Discovery Works

Substack has built-in features that help readers discover new publications. These include:

  • Recommendations: Other creators can recommend you to their readers. This feature is one of the best ways to get new subscribers to your page.

articles.title: Want to Sell an Agency? Launch a Creator Marketing Firm
articles.fullContent:
Creator agency M&A hit a record 30 acquisitions in 2026 as pandemic-era boutiques matured.

Private equity firms like Shamrock Capital and Velocity Capital are investing majority stakes in creator shops.

B2B creator marketing emerged as its own category this year, with firms like Freeman & Forrest helping tech companies reach technical audiences through creators.

Beta · Generated by AI, reviewed by ADWEEK newsroom This story was originally published in On Background with Mark Stenberg, a free weekly newsletter that explores the key themes shaping the media industry. You can sign up for it here .

In recent months, the market for creator and social agencies has been, to put it lightly, brisk.

In September, the Madrid-based social agency Samy acquired Get Engaged , a U.S. social and influencer shop, in a deal valued in the low nine figures.

In October, Billion Dollar Boy Group bought Creator Authority , a business-to-business influencer agency, and the private equity firm Shamrock Capital, which owns ADWEEK, made an eight-figure investment in the social-first agency Saylor .

Earlier this month, the social-first agency LV8 merged with its sister company Mirage Digital on the back of a “high eight figures” investment from Velocity Capital Management. And last week, the private equity firm Falfurrias Management Partners took a majority stake in Freeman & Forrest , another B2B creator agency.

The deals are part of a record year, according to James Creech, founder of the creator M&A advisory firm Quartermast. There have been 30 agency acquisitions in the creator economy so far in 2026, up from 20 in all of 2025 and above the previous high of 28 in 2022, according to Quartermast data.

Overall, there have been 124 M&A creator-adjacent deals this year, the busiest on record, and roughly half of the agency deals have come since July, per Quartermast.

Behind the surge is a crop of boutiques founded during the pandemic-era influencer boom that have matured into businesses worth buying, which are run by founders who need more resources to keep up with what clients are asking for.

A specific set of firms—social-first creative shops, podcast agencies, TikTok Shop specialists, and B2B creator plays—are responsible for the majority of this interest, while the deals themselves are increasingly financed by a new cohort of buyers, including private equity firms, strategic roll-ups, and international firms. All of it is unfolding in a frothy market for creator economy deals, which is just now beginning to consolidate in response to urgent demand across a fragmented space.

“Creator marketing works,” Creech said. “Brands and their agency partners are going to continue to invest there.”

The current rush of creator agency activity has its origins in the pandemic, according to LV8 chief executive Griffin Haddrill.

Lockdown acted as a digital accelerant, pulling budgets toward creators at a moment when television and film had dried up and out-of-home advertising had stopped working.

Because acquisitions typically take nine to 12 months to come together, the resulting deal volume spiked in 2021 and 2022, slowed over the following two years, and has since normalized, Creech said.

The same period produced a wave of new agencies, many of which were founded by executives who saw the emerging relevance of the creator ecosystem and launched startups to service it. Five years later, those boutiques have matured into businesses worth buying, according to Haddrill.

FOR Scoops, Sharp Analysis, and Insider Context

For founders, selling offers the resources to keep up with clients, according to Get Engaged co-founder Ben Hiott.

“Social is becoming the center of how brands build their businesses, and clients are asking us to do more every year,” Hiott said in October.

The wave of dealmaking that followed the pandemic was primarily influencer agencies, according to Creech, while this year, the variety of targets has expanded.

In 2026, buyers have gone after social-first creative agencies, such as Get Engaged, OK Cool, and Sway Social; podcast and audio shops like Ad Results Media and Listening Party Agency; and TikTok Shop specialists including Orca, Uptickk, and Yada.

Private equity is also getting more involved in the space, investing capital after years of financing strategic acquirers, as Bridgepoint does with Samy, according to Creech. This year, Shamrock Capital took a majority stake in Saylor, Velocity became a near-equal partner in LV8, and Falfurrias bought Freeman & Forrest, among other deals.

Serial acquirers are consolidating the field as well. Influencer agency Ykone has made four acquisitions in 2026, and creator company network Residence has made two, while Samy and Publicis remain active, according to Creech. After large platform deals for Influential and Captiv8, Publicis has turned to regional acquisitions, including the French creator agency Point d’Orgue, to enter new markets, according to Creech.

For investors, the opportunity lies in stitching these shops together, according to Haddrill.

“The consumer demand was there, but the agency space was fragmented,” Haddrill said. “Now, investors are seeing this fragmentation and working to bring them together.”

B2B creator marketing has also emerged as its own category.

Creator Authority, whose clients include Amazon, Adobe, and Mastercard, was Billion Dollar Boy Group’s first acquisition, an all-cash, multimillion-dollar deal with an earnout component, according to Business Insider .

She began her marketing career at Procter & Gamble after earning her MBA from Duke and later joined Georgia-Pacific, where she has spent 18 years across brand management, category leadership and marketing capability roles.

Today, her focus is on combining classic brand-building fundamentals with the data, technology and operating models needed for modern CPG marketing.

Private Label Is Waiting, So What About Your Brand? — Laura points out that consumers have been adjusting their behavior for years, not reacting to one sudden economic moment. In household essentials, private-label options are credible and easy to access. There’s a warning lying there for marketers: if the brand does not create a real reason to choose it, loyalty becomes much harder to defend.

100 Data Sources, One Source of Truth, Eighteen Months of Work — When Laura stepped into her current role, Georgia-Pacific needed to become more digitally capable. The first step was not another tool. It was fixing the data. Over 18 months, the team connected roughly 100 different sources, cleaned and harmonized them, and built one accessible system that now powers multiple in-house capabilities.

But the conclusion was the same: strong fundamentals work for both.

articles.title: Organic vs paid social media: Everything you need to know
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Organic social media builds trust and community without ad spend. The tradeoff is that reach is limited by platform algorithms.
  2. Paid social media scales reach fast and drives measurable results. It also requires ongoing budget and constant optimization.
  3. The strongest strategies combine both. Use organic to find what resonates, then use paid to scale it.
  4. Measuring organic and paid side by side gives you the full picture. When the two are reported separately, it’s almost impossible to tell what’s actually driving results.

What is organic social media?

Organic social media is the free content a person or brand posts on social platforms to connect with an audience. It includes content like Reels, Stories, TikToks, community replies, LinkedIn updates, and YouTube videos — any content you share without paying to promote it.

Organic social media activities include:

  • Sharing non-boosted content to your social media feeds
  • Encouraging your team to share company content on their own feeds (employee advocacy)
  • Engaging with your audience by responding to comments and DMs
  • Sharing user-generated content (UGC) that your community has organically shared with their own followers

Who sees organic social media content?

When you post organic content, it’s typically shown to:

  • A percentage of your followers (your “organic reach”)
  • People who visit your social media profile
  • Your followers’ followers (if they share your content)
  • People following relevant hashtags
  • People who see your content by platform algorithms (i.e., “suggested content”)

What is organic social media used for?

Organic social media is used to grow and engage an audience without paying to promote content, and it’s the foundation of any social media strategy. In practice, organic content can:

  • Generate awareness and conversation around your products or services
  • Show off your brand personality and voice
  • Build relationships with informative, entertaining, or inspiring content
  • Engage leads at every stage of the buying journey
  • Support customers with customer service

The common thread: organic isn’t about the hard sell, it’s about showing up in ways people actually want to engage with.

Each of these posts was shared organically to the brand’s feed so that people who land on your social media profile or are shown your post in their home feed are able to see it.

What are the benefits of organic social media?

The main benefit of organic social media is the ability to build relationships with your audience over time. Organic social media also helps:

  • Build trust and authority with your audience
  • Maintain a social media presence without ad spend
  • Support community engagement and loyalty

Build trust and authority with your audience

Organic social media builds trust because no one wants to feel pummeled by endless online advertisements.

Because organic content isn’t designed to push a conversion, it gives you more room to:

  • Share opinions and perspectives
  • Show up in a more authentic, human voice
  • Build brand awareness over time

As Peter Murphy Lewis, Fractional CMO at Strategic Pete, puts it, “Organic is where your voice, values, and vibe come through. It’s where your audience says, ‘I like how this brand thinks.’ It creates that layer of trust.”

TL;DR: Showing up consistently helps people see your brand as more than just a transaction, and that’s what keeps them coming back.

Maintain a social media presence without ad spend

One of the biggest advantages of organic social media is that it doesn’t require an advertising budget. Anyone can create a social media account and start posting with free social media tools and no upfront costs.

That doesn’t mean it’s effortless. Organic social still takes time and consistency, but the payoff compounds. Organic content can:

  • Continue generating engagement long after you hit “publish”
  • Reach new audiences organically through sharing or algorithmic discovery
  • Grow in value as your following increases

articles.title: Ubersuggest vs. Semrush vs. Ahrefs: Which SEO Tool Is Best?
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Ubersuggest starts at $29 a month and gives most small businesses what they need to find keywords and improve their rankings.
  • Semrush does a lot more than SEO. If you’re also running paid campaigns or managing social media, the higher price may be worth it.
  • Choose Ahrefs for serious backlink research. You can dig into who’s linking to your competitors and find opportunities that’d take a lot longer to uncover manually.
  • Moz’s Domain Authority metric is an industry standard, and Moz Local is a solid add-on if local search visibility is a priority.
  • Pay attention to AI search tracking. All four platforms now offer this, but coverage varies by plan. Check what your subscription includes before assuming you’re covered.
  • More features don’t automatically mean better results. Pick a tool that helps you get your SEO work done rather than pay extra for reports you’ll rarely open.

If you’re looking for SEO help, chances are you’ve come across online tools like Ubersuggest, Semrush, Ahrefs, and Moz. They’re four of the biggest names in SEO software, and they all promise to help you improve your search rankings.

Which ones are actually worth using, though?

Well, it depends on what you need from your SEO tool. What you’re willing to spend on certain capabilities and features is also a factor.

Some of these platforms pack in deep data and advanced functionality at a hefty price point. Others prioritize simplicity and speed so you can find opportunities and act on them without spending hours learning the software first.

Just because a tool has more features doesn’t necessarily mean it’s the better choice for you and your business. As I said, it really comes down to what you need.

Now, before we move forward, I should be upfront about something: I own Ubersuggest.

I acquired Ubersuggest and built it out because I wanted to make SEO more accessible, especially for people who don’t have hundreds of dollars to spend every month on software.

I also know Ubersuggest isn’t the right fit for everyone.

So, in this Ubersuggest vs. Semrush vs. Ahrefs vs. Moz comparison, we’ll cover what each tool does well and where each falls short. We’ll also help you figure out which one makes the most sense for your SEO needs.

And if you’re still newish to SEO, check out my SEO basics guide before diving in.

Ubersuggest vs. Semrush vs. Ahrefs vs. Moz: At a Glance

Before we get into the nitty-gritty, here’s a quick rundown of what each tool brings to the table. 

    Ubersuggest

    Let’s start with Ubersuggest, which is my SEO platform. I’ve built it out to make keyword research and SEO analysis accessible without a big budget.

    It helps you find keyword opportunities and check your site’s SEO health. It’s particularly useful for freelancers and small businesses that want actionable insights without a steep learning curve.

    Semrush

    Semrush is a comprehensive digital marketing platform that goes well beyond SEO. It includes tools for paid advertising and social media management, making it a strong option for bigger marketing teams.

Key takeaways

  1. What is a content approval workflow? It’s the step-by-step system for reviewing, editing, and approving content before it goes live, covering stages from drafting through final sign-off.
  2. Why do approval workflows fail? The most common reasons are scattered feedback, unclear ownership, and post-approval changes that bypass the process.

What is content approval?

Content approval is the process of reviewing and signing off on a piece of content before it gets published or distributed. It brings structure to the creative process so that posts, pages, and campaigns don’t slip through with typos, broken links, or off-brand messaging.

The content approval workflow usually starts with a draft (written by a content creator or strategist), moves through internal reviews, and ends with final sign-off. In some cases, there may also be feedback loops, legal review, or design tweaks along the way.

Most approval workflows follow these core stages:

  1. Ideate: Brainstorm content topics, campaigns, and messaging angles.
  2. Draft: Write copy, select visuals, and add links or hashtags.
  3. Review: An editor, peer, or manager checks for quality, accuracy, and brand alignment.
  4. Revise: The creator incorporates feedback and updates the draft.
  5. Approve: A final approver (or approval chain) signs off on the content.
  6. Publish/schedule: The approved post goes live or is queued for publishing.

In short, a content approval process gives every piece of content a clear path from idea to publish, with the right people reviewing at the right time.

Bonus: Download our bundle of free customizable social media workflow templates and set up a clear approval process for your team in minutes.

How does content approval work for social media?

Social media approval follows the same six stages, but the pace is different. You’re often reviewing dozens of short pieces a week rather than a handful of long ones, which means the process has to be fast enough to keep up with your publishing schedule without becoming a rubber stamp.

Social also adds a few wrinkles that other content types don’t have. Reviewers need to see platform-specific formatting (character limits, image crops, link previews) before they approve, not after. And because posts invite real-time replies, approvers are often signing off on timing and tone as much as copy.

Good workflows are built for how your team actually works. They account for your team size, your publishing cadence, and how your stakeholders prefer to communicate. The goal isn’t to over-engineer the process. It’s to keep your social media strategy moving smoothly and avoid last-minute surprises.

How does content approval extend beyond social media?

The same principles apply to website copy, blog posts, email campaigns, product pages, and digital assets like video or design files. The stages rarely change. What changes is the number of reviewers, the turnaround time, and how much technical or legal review each asset needs.

The examples in this guide focus on social media because that’s where volume and speed create the most friction. But if you’re building a workflow for other content types, the structure, roles, and tooling advice all carry over.

What makes a good content approval process?

People

  • Publishing timeline: A plan that shows when posts are due and when they go live.
  • Deadlines (internal and external): Keeps everyone on track, especially for launches, events, or client work.
  • Audit trail and version history: Keep a record of who changed what, and when, so you can trace decisions and roll back if needed.

Tools

  • Reliable notification system: Make sure the right people are pinged at the right time (not buried in Slack threads).

  • Error-checking apps: Use tools that catch broken links, spelling errors, or duplicate posts before they go out.

Key Takeaways

  • Choose keywords based on user intent rather than on search volume or traffic alone. 
  • Check your keyword rankings in Google Search Console to see which searches bring up your pages and where you have opportunities to improve. 
  • Before targeting a keyword, evaluate its monthly search volume (MSV), cost-per-click (CPC), ranking difficulty, and AI Overview presence to understand its traffic potential and competitiveness.
  • AI Overviews can reduce organic click-through rates (CTRs) by answering questions directly in search results. That makes traditional rankings a less reliable measure of potential traffic. 
  • Create useful content around related keywords that share the same search intent. Don’t try to force unrelated terms and topics onto one page. 
  • Improving your organic rankings can also increase your chances of being cited in Google’s AI Overviews. That gives your content another opportunity to reach potential customers.

Chances are, you want more website traffic. After all, more traffic means more business revenue, right?

Not necessarily.

More traffic’s all well and good, but attracting the wrong audience won’t do much for your bottom line. Instead, focus on improving traffic quality by targeting high-intent keywords that attract people who are more likely to buy.

Why? Consider this: The No. 1 Google search result for a given query has an average click-through rate (CTR) of 20.9 percent. Compare this with a CTR of less than 1 percent for results in spot No. 10.

Ranking first doesn’t guarantee the traffic it once did, however. The presence of a Google AI Overview in your search results is associated with a 58 percent lower average CTR for the top-ranking organic result. That’s compared to stats from just two years ago.

Despite this, ranking at the top still matters. It’s now just part of a more complex equation.

With this in mind, let’s take a look at how keyword ranking for SEO works. I’ll cover how to check your current rankings, then discuss how to choose the right keywords for your content to improve SEO keyword rankings.

What Is Keyword Ranking in SEO?

An SEO “keyword” refers to a word or phrase someone types into a search engine like Google or Bing. Ideally, the search engine will respond with results that match what the user is looking for. Your position within these results is your “keyword ranking” for the given search query.

It’s important to remember your ranking does not indicate your placement in Google’s AI Overview, however.

Here’s what current research tells us about how people search and which keywords get traffic:

  • Nearly 93 percent of keywords in Ahrefs’ U.S. database are searched more than 10 times a month.
  • Question-based searches increased from 8 percent in 2023 to 21 percent in 2026.
  • Search queries are becoming more conversational. Three- and four-word keywords made up 48 percent of search impressions in 2026, a 15 percent increase.

Say you sell electric hand mixers and write a product category page for your products. Think about what keywords people type into Google to find your product. For example, they might search for something like “buy electric hand mixer.”

As I mentioned earlier, your SEO keyword ranking is the spot your page occupies in the list of Google search results. In this case, KitchenAid ranks above articles about the best hand mixers.

Search engine results pages (SERPs) keep changing, though. Today, these organic results often sit below product and local business listings related to this keyword. AI Overviews often display answers and explanations above organic listings.

Still, the No. 1 organic result remains the position with the most value. 

SEO, or search engine optimization, involves optimizing your content using the right keywords to improve your page ranking. Let’s check out why this is important.

Why Are SEO Keyword Rankings Important?

Organic searches drive traffic. In fact, NP Digital data suggests that about 41 percent of traffic comes from organic search queries. That figure varies by industry and dataset, and some recent studies put it lower. 

Even as organic search’s share of traffic declines slightly, it remains the No. 1 source for website traffic.

articles.fullContent:
Over the last decade, social media has rapidly evolved alongside new technologies, AI and the content creator landscape. Social media networks now function as brand PR channels, customer service platforms and community building tools simultaneously. And while you balance all those pieces, consumers expect you to create an active, authentic online presence that resonates with them.

Complicating matters, your brand presence extends beyond your main account pages. In a Sprout Social Q2 2026 Pulse Survey, 40% of respondents said they found employee-generated content (EGC) to be more authentic than posts on the brand’s page. EGC (and all influencer content) is powerful but needs the right safeguards in place to maintain the reputation of your brand and its values.

Implementing a social media policy will help protect your company, navigate AI, prioritize consumer privacy and give employees the space to advocate for themselves.

Please note: The information provided in this article does not, and is not intended to, constitute formal legal advice. Please review our full disclaimer before reading any further.

What is a company social media policy?

A social media policy is part of a company’s business code of conduct that tells employees how they should represent themselves and the brand on social media. Policy differs from social media guidelines, which are best practices for using specific social channels. Policy includes protocols to protect the brand’s security, privacy and legal interests.

Social media platforms provide avenues for brand promotion, but they also present opportunities to misrepresent your brand, which is why a good social media policy is so necessary. Many policies also now include guidelines around whether AI-generated content is okay to use on social, how to label it and how the policy ties to broader company AI guardrails.

If you’d like to see how a social media policy is structured, download our free template.

Why do you need a social media policy for employees?

Here are several reasons organizations should adopt a social media policy:

Safely amplify employee voices

Employees, both intentionally and unintentionally, have become a new type of social media influencer. As they share about their work experiences, brand promotions and company behind-the-scenes, their content is getting in front of customers. According to the Sprout Social Influencer Marketing Report, more than half of consumers are seeing content from brand employees at least once a week, and 15% are seeing it daily.

Consumers are excited about EGC, with 46% saying they want to hear from frontline employees specifically. When your employees post about the organization online, it can increase brand awareness, establish thought leadership and drive qualified leads. Along with helping social selling, employee posts can support social recruiting efforts, attracting top talent to your company.

Yet, EGC does come with inherent risks; an unhappy employee with a following can quickly create a brand crisis. Team members not trained in brand voice may misrepresent the company. Social media policies allow you to unlock all the benefits of employee advocacy, without putting your brand credibility at risk. Your social media policy is a critical advocacy tool, giving your employees the guidance they need to represent your brand accurately within social networks. This is a key component of social media governance, ensuring consistent and responsible online behavior across your organization.

Having sensible guidelines in place ensures employees can post in their unique voices while still maintaining brand safety.

Promote DEI

Brand diversity in social media is more important than ever. Consumers want to interact with and purchase from brands that share their values.

Amplifying diverse voices via social media is an actionable step brands can take to prioritize representation and attract top talent from marginalized communities. An inclusive social media policy will empower and encourage voices from all backgrounds to advocate for the brand.

Maintain a consistent brand identity

A social media policy ensures that whenever someone interacts with your company online, either through a brand channel or an employee, they get the same consistent experience. This develops a more reliable, trustworthy identity for your company, turning customers into loyal fans and ambassadors.

Minimize legal action against your brand

Social media presents complicated considerations such as privacy law and copyright law. A well made social media policy will protect the company from potential lawsuits.

Consult with your legal counsel and outline a list of do’s and don’ts for the company to follow. These rules of thumb will help ensure the organization and contractors are compliant with laws, reducing the risk of legal action against the company.

Protect your brand from privacy and security risks

Privacy and security concerns on social media are growing, affecting your brand and audiences. How you secure your accounts and protect customer information on these channels is critical. The Q1 2026 pulse survey found that when users experienced an increase in social media trust, it was most often thanks to improvements in security and privacy protocols.

Work to close any security gaps in your social media approach. A good social media policy combined with security protocols will protect your accounts against hacking, phishing and fraud accounts.

And since social media is a common resource for scammers and criminals, it’s imperative your social media policy includes guidelines that protect your employees and company. Whether it’s defending against phishing scams or ransomware attacks, make sure that everyone in your organization is vigilant about online protection.

Prevent a public relations crisis

Many organizations make the mistake of waiting until they’ve faced a public relations disaster to put a policy in place. Be proactive and implement a strategy in advance to minimize crises and the costs that come with one.

Social media is the number one place consumers first hear of an unfolding brand crisis, according to the Q2 2026 Sprout Social Pulse Survey. Around 64% of consumers surveyed want brands to respond publicly to a crisis on social media instead of via press release or a website announcement, so be sure to lay out a response framework well in advance.

Your social media crisis plan should align with your social media policy. For example, the policy can designate which teams are responsible for handling a PR crisis.

What is a social media style guide?

A social media style guide is a document that defines how your brand looks, sounds, and behaves across every social platform. It covers everything from your visual identity (e.g., your logo and color palette) to your tone of voice, and even how you use emojis and hashtags. Some teams call it social media brand guidelines, but the purpose is the same.

These days, a style guide covers more than what your core social team publishes. It also governs AI-generated drafts, content shared by employees, and work coming from agencies or regional teams.

A strong style guide works alongside your social media strategy, translating high-level goals into the day-to-day rules your team actually follows.

You search for your own business from your desk and there it is, number two on the map. Looks great.

Meanwhile, someone standing six blocks east types the same words into their phone, and you are nowhere on the list. A customer a mile north sees you at number 14. Same keyword, same business, completely different results, depending on where the searcher happens to be standing.

A single rank number cannot describe that. Ubersuggest built the Local SEO Checker to show the whole picture: your Google Maps rank at up to 81 points around your business, laid out on one map.

What Is a Google Maps Rank Checker?

A Google Maps rank checker shows where a business appears in Google Maps results for a keyword. Ubersuggest’s Local SEO Checker does this across a grid of points rather than from one location. It simulates a search from each point’s exact location, then plots your rank at every point on a single map, so you can see which neighborhoods find you and which ones do not.

That grid matters because Google favors businesses closer to the searcher. Ranking in local results depends on relevance, distance, and prominence, and distance changes with every step the customer takes. Your rank at your front door tells you very little about your rank two miles away.

Why Does Your Local Rank Change From Block to Block?

Your rank changes by location because Google puts more weight on businesses close to the person searching. Move the searcher, and the order of results moves with them.

Picture a coffee shop. Search “coffee shop near me” from the shop’s own street and it may sit at the top of the map. Search from a neighborhood a mile away, where three other cafés sit on the corner, and the same shop might drop to the second page or vanish.

The owner who only ever checks from the shop never sees that. The result is a strange kind of blind spot: the business looks healthy from its own doorstep while whole neighborhoods of potential customers never see it.

For agencies and consultants, the problem takes a different shape. A client asks “how is my business doing on Google Maps?” and the honest answer is “it depends where.” A grid replaces that shrug with a picture.

How Does the Local SEO Checker Work?

You run a scan in four steps, and the map fills in point by point as it runs.

  1. Find your business. Search by name and pick it from the Google Maps suggestions. If the business is in another city, set the location field first.
  2. Set up the grid. Choose a grid from 3×3 to 9×9, then the distance between points. Center it on your business or on any address. Distances run from ¼ to 2 miles, or ½ to 5 kilometers.
  3. Enter one keyword. Each scan checks a single keyword, such as “coffee shop near me.”
  4. Review and run. Check the credit cost and your balance, then run the scan.

The review screen lists the business, the scan center, the grid settings, the keyword, the total pins, the total scan cost, and your current balance. Nothing is charged before you confirm.

You can also center the grid on any address, including a neighborhood where you want to win customers but have not yet.

What Does the Grid Look Like, and What Do the Colors Mean?

The grid is a set of pins on a map, and each pin carries your rank at that point. The colors tell you the story at a glance:

  • Green: top 3
  • Yellow: 4 to 10
  • Red: 11 to 20
  • Dark brown: 21 or lower
  • Gray: not ranked

articles.fullContent:
Anyone who manages their company’s social media for a living operates every day in fear of being the one at the helm when the brand account is hacked. But many don’t know what steps to take to mitigate that fear.

While the biggest brand risk is not being present on social at all, we can’t deny the inherent security concerns of building and maintaining a digital footprint. There are so many new platforms emerging, so much content out there (including rampant misinformation) and mounting concerns about account access in the face of turnover. Brands must make social media governance a priority.

And AI is now the fastest-growing governance gap. Leaders are asking teams to adopt it faster than policies, approvals and vendor reviews can keep up, and this pressure is already showing: 39% of marketers say the social and political climate brought more restrictions on content and influencer partners, while 44% say it brought more internal approvals.

At its core, social media governance equates to one thing: eliminating risk. By putting proper processes and procedures in place and managing your social media accounts in a centralized manner, you significantly turn down the dial on the brand threat barometer.

If you need help making the argument for the resources you need to do governance well, keep reading. Here are the top risks of not creating a social media governance framework for your operation, and how to start implementing an effective strategy.

What is social media governance?

Social media governance is how an organization sets rules and responsibilities for using social media safely and effectively. It includes things like who can post on official accounts, who can use AI tools for defined reasons (including which tools to use and with what review), how to respond to customer questions or crises, the guidelines employees and influencers should follow when representing the brand online, and how to follow required security measures.

A thorough social media governance framework helps protect your brand’s reputation, stay compliant with legal and privacy requirements, and reduce the risk of mistakes or misuse. Creating clear approval processes for social posts, providing social media training, and monitoring for potential security threats or off-brand content are all examples of social media governance in action.

With threats like doxxing and increasingly sophisticated cyber attacks, the current state of the social industry makes governance an even more pressing issue. Between the rise of AI content and spread of misinformation, distributed and hybrid teams, social media professional turnover rates and increasingly sophisticated cyber threats, teams are up against continuous waves of risk.

Why social media governance is so important

While a social media governance framework isn’t the glamorous side of social, it is 100% necessary when it comes to protecting your brand and granting stakeholders (like your IT team) peace of mind. Here are nine reasons why social media governance matters.

1. Risk to your brand

Obviously, if hackers gain access to your social media accounts, they’re not there to respond to customer inquiries with winning service skills. Ask yourself how much damage would be done if criminals got control of your social media accounts and published something disparaging, changed your account to look like your primary competitor’s account or converted it over to make it look like it supports terrorist groups (note: all are real examples). How much would your credibility be damaged? And what about your brand?

2. Compliance and regulatory risk

Depending on your industry, you may have additional rules guiding what your company can and cannot say publicly. Companies in the financial, medical and pharmaceutical industries all have additional considerations. Even other industries like travel, energy and higher education are under increased scrutiny.

Industry aside, all companies have to worry about violating government regulations regarding social media. If you have trouble getting budget to support governance work, tell your leaders this could cost them $50 million (or more). Not paying attention to governance can land you in hot water with a number of regulatory agencies, from the FTC to the governing bodies in Europe that hand down GDPR fines. And you must be extra aware if you manage a widely recognized brand. Regulatory bodies will intentionally make an example out of major corporations to generate big headlines.

It’s only a matter of time until we have a US equivalent of GDPR. Currently 20 states have already instituted their own versions.

These risks are constantly evolving, with new legislative actions like the push for social media bans in the US and abroad presenting significant compliance hurdles for global brands.

3. Legal risk

As companies rely more on social media as a form of customer service and communication, chances are higher that lawsuits based on social media will emerge. If you cannot say definitively who had access to your accounts at a given time or who posted a specific item or comment, you may find yourself unable to defend yourself to your supervisors, your legal team or a court of law.

4. Human risk

To err may be human, but if the human happens to be a social media manager, forgiveness is a hard thing to come by. Bottom line, people absolutely make mistakes. But the proper tools and procedures make it a lot less likely that someone will accidentally post from the company account instead of their personal account or that they will do something else that causes you a self-imposed PR “incident.” It also saves you from having to fire someone.

5. Risk from your own employees (internal risks)

A lot of companies do not have firm rules about what employees are allowed to do on social media. Employees may accidentally share items that include confidential information (such as financial or HR data) or air personal grievances against the company or coworkers in a very public forum. Not having official policies and rules makes it hard to hold people accountable, and it makes it hard for employees to know what is and is not okay.

articles.title: GEO vs SEO vs AEO vs LLMO: What’s The Difference?
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • The choice between generative engine optimization (GEO) and search engine optimization (SEO) isn’t either-or. The two disciplines complement each other.
  • SEO earns rankings in traditional search results. GEO builds the depth and authority that earn your content citations in AI-generated answers across platforms like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google’s AI Overviews.
  • Answer engine optimization (AEO) and large language model optimization (LLMO) round out the picture. 
  • AEO helps structure your content to become the direct answer in AI-powered search experiences, from featured snippets to AI Overviews and tools like ChatGPT. LLMO shapes how large language models (LLMs) understand and describe your brand.
  • Google considers AI optimization “still SEO” because “optimizing for generative AI search is optimizing for the search experience.”
  • To build a combined strategy, start with your SEO foundation. From there, structure pages for AEO and deepen content for GEO. Consistent brand information across the web supports LLMO.

If you’ve been doing SEO for a while, you’ve probably noticed a shift. SEO is no longer the only factor to consider in search visibility. 

According to Ahrefs research, Google’s AI Overviews are associated with a 58 percent lower click-through rate for top-ranking pages.

AI-powered search is reaching a massive audience. Google reports that AI Overviews has more than 2.5 billion monthly users, while AI Mode has already passed 1 billion monthly users.

At the same time, people are skipping Google altogether and using tools like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini for answers and recommendations. 

That’s created a wave of new terminology: GEO, SEO, AEO, LLMO, and so on. Keeping it up with it all can feel overwhelming.

Each covers a different search surface that SEO wasn’t built for. They don’t replace SEO, but you also can’t rely on SEO alone.

I get questions all the time about how SEO, GEO, AEO, and LLMO relate to one another and when each one matters. If you’re asking those same questions, this guide is for you. We’ll start with GEO vs. SEO as the foundation, then layer AEO and LLMO on top.

Defining the Four Disciplines

SEO, GEO, AEO, and LLMO each target a different surface:

  • Generative engine optimization focuses on getting AI tools to cite or recommend your content in their answers. Those include Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini.   • Answer engine optimization helps your site appear as a direct answer in search results. That covers featured snippets, People Also Ask boxes, knowledge panels, voice assistant responses, and AI-generated answers in tools like ChatGPT and Google’s AI Overviews. AEO relies on clear, structured content, like FAQs and schema markup. It’s ideal for high-intent, question-based queries.
  • Large language model optimization shapes how AI models understand and describe your brand. LLMO is built on clear entities and original insights paired with a consistent brand presence across platforms.

Each discipline works differently and measures success differently. Here’s how they compare side by side.

Here’s where they connect:

  • Structure increases visibility. Descriptive headers and short paragraphs help crawlers and AI models process your content. Ordered lists and clear tables are especially useful for queries where users need to compare options or follow steps.

A great product or clever marketing campaign might get someone interested in your business. But what convinces them to buy, recommend it to a friend or come back for more? It comes down to brand trust.

Consumers are getting more particular about where they place that trust. With AI-generated content raising new questions about what’s real, many are looking closer at product claims and seeking honest opinions from other customers. According to Sprout Social’s Q2 2026 Pulse Survey, 57% of consumers trust everyday product users most for recommendations, far ahead of subject matter experts (26%), mega-influencers (9%) and brand employees (8%).

This shift gives brands a chance to rethink how they earn consumer confidence. People want to know a business will deliver on its promises, and their experiences with a brand often speak louder than any marketing campaign. For brands that get it right, the payoff extends well beyond the initial sale.

Brand trust develops over time, shaped by everything from how a company communicates to how it handles customer concerns. Understanding what earns trust is essential to building lasting relationships.

Read on to learn what brand trust means today, why it matters for business growth and how to build, measure and maintain it.

What is brand trust?

Brand trust is consumers’ confidence in a business and its ability to meet their expectations. Several factors shape that confidence, including:

  • Your brand values and mission
  • The quality of your products or services
  • Transparency around business practices and supply chains (e.g., AI disclaimers, certifications, eco-friendly, etc.)
  • The honesty of your advertising claims (e.g., health claims, product longevity, research efficacy)
  • Your treatment of employees and manufacturers
  • An authentic brand voice that reflects your business’s values
  • Responsible, brand-safe influencer partnerships
  • Reliable customer service and care

Building trust means consistently following through on these commitments. Customers notice when a brand’s actions match its messaging, and when there’s a disconnect.

Authenticity plays an important role here. According to Sprout Social’s Q3 2026 Pulse Survey, authenticity is the number one trait consumers value in brands on social media. That desire for authenticity extends beyond social media. Consumers want to see the same honesty reflected in how a business operates and treats its customers.

Your reputation also matters to future buyers, too. A strong track record can give potential customers the confidence to choose your brand, even if they’re unfamiliar with your products or services.

Why is building brand trust important for a strong brand?

Brand trust is more than a “feel-good” goal. It’s a concrete way to drive profitability and expansion. While no brand can maintain a perfect reputation all the time, those that earn consumers’ trust over the long term are better positioned to compete and succeed in their industry.

Enhanced loyalty and retention

When consumers trust your brand, they’re more likely to choose your products over competitors. Positive experiences reinforce that confidence, helping improve customer retention and reduce churn.

Product quality plays a major role in maintaining trust and loyalty. According to Sprout Social’s Q3 2026 Pulse Survey, 44% of consumers say product or service quality is their top driver of brand loyalty. Consistently meeting customer expectations gives them a reason to stick around, even when other options are available.

Customer advocacy and evangelism

Trustworthy brands benefit from higher levels of customer advocacy, leading to valuable word-of-mouth recommendations and a stronger brand reputation. Brand trust can differentiate your brand from competitors, attract new customers, and create opportunities for future partnerships and collaborations.

This advocacy isn’t limited to customers; it can be even more impactful when it comes from key opinion leaders and thought leaders whose expert endorsements can strengthen a brand’s reputation.

Increased customer lifetime value

When consumers trust brands, they’re more likely to keep engaging over time, make repeat purchases, and upgrade to higher-value products or services. Consumers who trust a brand are also more likely to recognize the value of its products and services, making them more willing to pay a premium for the quality and experience they expect.

Building brand trust should be a key part of your wider customer retention strategy. Nurturing relationships over time can increase customer lifetime value and support more sustainable business growth.

How to build brand trust

While understanding what brand trust means is relatively straightforward, building it is much more complex. It requires a coordinated effort across your business, from internal operations to how you communicate with customers. Every department plays a role in earning and maintaining consumer confidence.

Maintain a consistent brand voice across communication channels

Consistent brand messaging helps customers recognize your business and know what to expect. Whether someone encounters your brand through an ad, visits your website or receives a marketing email, the underlying message should feel familiar.

Establish clear brand guidelines that define your tone of voice, visual identity and core messaging. These guidelines help teams stay consistent across campaigns and channels while adapting their approach to different audiences and formats.

Its colorful packaging, playful illustrations and bold typography appear across channels, while its conversational, humorous copy gives the brand a consistent personality. Key Takeaways

  • Visibility and accuracy fail independently. An engine can cite you in nearly every answer and still describe you with outdated facts.
  • Score three axes, not one verdict. Rate each brand-relevant answer on accuracy, sentiment, and currency. Each axis points to a different fix.
  • Answers drift for documented reasons. Engines surface the most repeated claim. Source content that passed through unsupervised AI editing can arrive already degraded.
  • No platform offers an edit button. ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, and Perplexity accept feedback. None commits to changing a specific answer.
  • Source correction carries the most weight. Fixing the pages an engine cites changes the answer more reliably than any in-product report.

Every AI visibility report answers one question: are you showing up, and how often? Rank tracking, citation counts, and visibility measured at scale all count appearances. None of them tell you what the answer said about you. That blind spot is where AI sentiment and accuracy live.

Your brand can hold a strong citation rate across ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, and Perplexity while the answer describes a product you sunset two years ago. The same answer might credit a competitor with your flagship feature, or lead with a complaint from a single review site. Your dashboard still shows green.

Visibility tells you whether you are in the conversation. Sentiment and accuracy tell you whether that helps you or hurts you. This post covers how to score both, why answers go stale, and which correction levers do real work.

Visibility Tells You If You’re in the Room. It Doesn’t Tell You What Was Said.

Citation frequency, inclusion rate, and share of voice all measure presence. An engine can name you in nine of 10 answers and still get your pricing model wrong in all nine. AI brand misrepresentation sits outside what any visibility metric detects.

Four situations call for different work.

High visibility, accurate answers. You are in good shape. Keep monitoring, because engines refresh their sources constantly.

High visibility, inaccurate answers. Your worst case, and the one a dashboard hides. The engine repeats you often and repeats you wrong, so every citation amplifies the error.

Low visibility, accurate answers. A reach problem. You need more citable, authoritative coverage. NP Digital’s study of 9 million AI answers found that owned citations deliver the single strongest visibility lift in the data.

Low visibility, inaccurate answers. Two jobs at once. Fix the source material first, then push for citations, or you will scale the wrong story.

In the past, this site has covered how AI answers compress a brand’s first impression, and how defending your brand in AI results starts with governance. That piece explains the problem. This one gives you the scoring system, because you cannot govern what you have not measured.

A quarterly report with rising citation counts can cover a quarter in which your reputation got worse. The numbers improve while the answers degrade, and nothing in the report connects the two.

Why AI Answers Drift Out of Date and Out of Alignment

Two documented mechanisms explain most of what an audit turns up. Neither one is a conspiracy against your brand. Both are structural.

Engines Weight Repetition, Not Verification

Language models surface the claim that appears most consistently across their sources. A hundred directory pages carrying your 2021 address outweigh one corrected About page, and the engine cannot tell which version is true. Confident phrasing says nothing about input quality. The Tow Center for Digital Journalism tested eight AI search tools and found that they answered more than 60 percent of queries incorrectly. Perplexity performed best, and still got 37 percent wrong. Every wrong answer arrived in the same assured tone as a right one. Our own NP Digital has shown that nearly half of marketers deal with AI errors multiple times a week.

  3. Act on your insights by reaching your audience on more networks, with less manual work

With each step, we dug into the Sprout capabilities that gave teams an edge this year and the newest releases that will help set-up your 2027 strategy.

Trellis enhancements 

Ask Trellis, your AI teammate, a question in plain language and get themes, trends and recommended next steps, with examples to back them up. Start broad with something like: “What drove the most engagement this year?” Then keep going: “What’s worth doubling down on? What could we try next?” Trellis builds on each answer, so you can keep asking until you know the best next move.

And with new platform-wide search, you can look up your tags, labels, users and profiles in one place. Just ask what you want to know, and Trellis pulls in the right data behind the scenes.

It reads news and web coverage in the context of your brand, so you can see how a story lands for your brand, track the key messages you care about and give leadership a clear answer to “What does this coverage mean for us?”

Simply putting a form on a landing page doesn’t guarantee people will submit. 

One study showed that more than half of people who visit a form fail to successfully complete it. Since forms are a gateway to lead generation, that’s a lot of missed opportunity. 

Why aren’t people clicking or completing?

If you don’t optimize your forms for users, they’re more likely to abandon them or not even click into them at all.

So, how do you increase form conversions?

A few tweaks like form placement, field count, color, and copy can turn your forms into a key driver of lead generation, which is exactly what this article will cover. Read on to start generating the leads you need to scale and grow. 

1. Place the Form Where It Gets Seen

Form placement dictates how many visitors see your form. Attention still clusters at the top of the page, where users spend more time. That said, placement should shift based on factors like user intent and what you’re asking visitors to commit to. 

Industry plays a role, too. B2B brands, for example, typically see higher average time spent on page than retail brands.

Why?

Higher-intent users, like those shopping for a specific product at a store, tend to convert better on shorter pages. They know what they want (and they want it fast). A call-to-action (CTA) or form makes sense at the very top of the page, or even as a pop-up.  

Gap.com, for instance, uses a pop-up to capture user attention with a 15 percent-off discount.

Saving money doesn’t need much explanation, so it makes sense to put this front and center.

Lower-intent users want more information before making a decision, especially for complex products or services, such as booking a software demo. They need to understand what you do and why it matters to them.

Users get a clear view of what Deel does and can consider their services before booking a demo.

A smaller device like a phone could push the form down below other elements like the header or hero image, and users may never even see it.

2. Ensure You Have a Strong Call-to-Action

The call-to-action is the tipping point between conversions and bounce. It drives action and conversions, which is what you want.

Not all CTAs do the job well, however. Something as simple as a word or color can affect conversion rates.  

For example, a button that says “Submit” asks for effort without a clear value proposition.
